opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that synthetic data generation and curation sound simple when you describe them. You take some seed data, you call an LLM, you get outputs, you filter them. But once you try to do it at any real scale, you run into a lot of practical pain, and a tool like Curator should take that pain away so people can focus on the data itself.

The first thing is making it easy to express a pipeline. You want to say: here's my prompt, here's how I want the response structured, here's how I want to parse it into rows. That should be a few lines of code, not a whole engineering project. Structured outputs matter a lot here, because you often want a list of questions, or a reasoning trace plus a final answer, and you want those to land cleanly in a dataset.

The second thing is scale and reliability. If you're generating hundreds of thousands or millions of examples, you'll hit rate limits, failed requests, malformed responses, and so on. So the tool needs to handle retries, concurrency, and batching. Batch APIs from the providers are much cheaper, so supporting them out of the box makes a big difference in cost. And caching is huge. If your job dies halfway through, or you tweak one step, you shouldn't have to pay to regenerate everything. You should be able to resume where you left off.

Third is flexibility across models. People want to try different providers, open models through something like vLLM, different sizes for different stages. Maybe a strong model for hard reasoning traces and a cheaper one for filtering. So you want one interface that works across all of them.

And finally, visibility. Data work is iterative. You need to look at what you're generating, see the failure modes, check costs and progress, and then adjust prompts or filters. So having a viewer, being able to inspect samples, and integrating with the ecosystem people already use, like Hugging Face datasets, is really important.

Underneath all of that is a broader belief: data is a huge lever for model quality, especially for post-training and reasoning. We saw that with our own work on reasoning datasets, where a relatively small, well-curated set can get you a long way. So the tool should make it really cheap to experiment with data, because the more experiments you can run, the better your data gets.

r001.rationale: The response discusses synthetic data generation and filtering, but does not distinguish filtering existing human data from generating synthetic data.

r002.rationale: It mentions batching and batch APIs, but does not contrast Curator’s offline, batch-oriented workflow with online tools designed for prompting models.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the way I think about it is that data curation for training models has become a fundamentally different activity than it was a few years ago. Historically, when people said "data curation," they meant something like: scrape the web, filter out the junk, dedupe it, maybe apply some quality classifiers. That's still important, but increasingly the data that actually moves the needle for post-training is synthetic. It's generated by models. And once you accept that, the tool you need looks a lot more like a software engineering tool than a data cleaning tool.

So when we built Curator, the thing we kept coming back to was: what does the actual workflow look like for someone building a dataset today? And it's usually some pipeline of LLM calls. You start with some seed, maybe a set of topics or documents or existing prompts. You call a model to generate questions. You call a model, often a different, stronger model, to generate answers or reasoning traces. Then you call a model to grade or filter those. And you iterate on this many, many times. The prompt changes, the model changes, the filtering threshold changes, and every time you touch something you want to see what came out.

The first thing a tool like that needs to provide is just making those pipelines easy to express. You shouldn't have to write a bunch of boilerplate around asynchronous requests and rate limits and retries and parsing structured outputs. That's all plumbing, and everyone was reinventing it badly. So we wanted it to be a few lines of Python: here's my prompt function, here's how I parse the response, run it over this dataset.

The second thing, and honestly this is the one I think gets underrated, is performance and cost. If you're generating a million samples, you're talking about real money and real wall-clock time. So the tool has to handle batching, it has to handle the batch APIs that OpenAI and Anthropic and others offer, which are dramatically cheaper, it has to be able to hit multiple backends, including open models that you're serving yourself with something like vLLM. If it only works with one provider at small scale, it's a demo, not a tool.

Third is caching. This sounds boring but it's a huge deal. When you're iterating on a pipeline, you change the last stage and you do not want to re-run the first three stages and pay for all those tokens again. So Curator caches aggressively at every step, and that makes the iteration loop fast and cheap, which in turn makes people experiment more, which is where the quality comes from.

And then the last piece is observability. When you're producing synthetic data, the failure modes are subtle. The model generates responses that are fine individually but all sound the same. Or your parser silently drops a third of the outputs. Or the grader is way too lenient. You need to actually look at the data. So we built a viewer where you can see the inputs, the outputs, the intermediate stages, and just read through samples. I really believe that if you're not looking at your data, you're not doing data curation, you're just running scripts.

So to put it together: easy to express pipelines, scales cheaply across providers, caching so iteration is fast, and tooling to actually inspect what you made. That's the core. And the reason we open-sourced it is that we were building these pipelines ourselves for things like our OpenThoughts work, and we realized the infrastructure was the bottleneck for a lot of other people too.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts traditional filtering and deduplication with model-generated synthetic data, but it does not clearly distinguish using an LLM to filter existing human data from using one to generate synthetic data.

r002.rationale: It describes pipelines, batching, and batch APIs, but does not contrast Curator’s offline workflow with online tools geared toward prompting models.

astra-6.text:
I think a data curation tool needs to help you answer three questions: What’s in my data? What’s useful for the model I’m trying to build? And what am I missing?

That starts with making the dataset easy to explore. You should be able to find similar examples, identify duplicates, and see where you have a lot of coverage versus very little. Then you need ways to act on that understanding—to select a representative subset, remove examples that aren’t useful, or find more examples of something your model struggles with.

The important thing is connecting that process back to model performance. A dataset can look clean and still be missing exactly the cases that matter for your application. So I think of curation as an iterative process: understand the data, make a change, train or evaluate the model, and use what you learn to guide the next change. The tool needs to make that loop easy.

r001.rationale: The response discusses exploring, selecting, removing, or finding examples, but does not distinguish filtering existing human data with an LLM from generating synthetic data.

r002.rationale: It describes an iterative curation loop but does not contrast an offline, batch-oriented workflow with online tools for prompting models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a data curation tool needs to help you understand your data first. What’s in the dataset? Where are the duplicates? What’s low quality, and what’s missing? When you have millions of images, you can’t answer those questions by looking at every example, so you need ways to search, visualize, and discover patterns at scale.

Then you need to be able to act on that understanding. You might want to remove duplicates, filter out irrelevant examples, or build a subset that’s more representative of the problem you’re trying to solve. And that depends on the use case. An image that’s useful for one model might not be useful for another, so the tool needs to give users control over those decisions.

Ultimately, you want to close the loop with model performance. Can you identify where the model struggles, find the data that addresses those gaps, and see whether the next version improves? That’s what makes curation an iterative part of building a model.

r001.rationale: The response describes exploring and filtering existing examples, but does not mention LLMs or distinguish that use from generating synthetic data.

r002.rationale: The response discusses curation at scale and iteration, but does not contrast an offline, batch-oriented Curator workflow with online tools for prompting models.
